detail.abstract: Unethical behavior remains a persistent challenge in organizations, yet less is known about how individuals' emotional capabilities shape the psychological processes underlying such misconduct. Drawing on social cognitive theory, we argue that emotional intelligence influences unethical behavior through moral disengagement and investigates whether job demands condition the relationship. To test the hypotheses, we conduct a two-wave survey of 409 full-time employees in China. The results reveal that emotional intelligence reduces moral disengagement, which subsequently decreases unethical behavior. However, job demands do not significantly moderate the relationship between emotional intelligence and moral disengagement. These findings extend research on workplace ethics by identifying emotional intelligence as an antecedent of moral self-regulation and specifying moral disengagement as a key mechanism through which emotional capabilities shape unethical conduct. Implications for both business ethics theory and practice are discussed.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence sits in growing tension with the planetary boundaries sustainability discourse defends. The IEA (2025) projects that data-centre electricity demand will roughly double to 945 TWh by 2030, and the water footprint of generative AI is rising in step. Yet policy and corporate responses treat AI as a sustainability solution rather than a sustainability problem, sustaining the techno-optimist framing recent work in sustainable AI has begun to contest (van Wynsberghe, 2021; Falk and van Wynsberghe, 2023). This paper argues that refusal, restraint and selective scaling are legitimate responsible-innovation strategies for enterprise AI adoption, and that the luxury sector is a productive empirical site for studying them. Luxury maisons operate under a commercial logic in which restraint creates value, which gives the sector an unusual capacity to absorb the strategic cost of not adopting AI at the pace and scope its developers propose. Drawing on the RI pillars of Stilgoe, Owen and Macnaghten (2013), the STS literature on technology non-adoption (Wyatt, 2005; Selwyn, 2003), and recent work on Green AI and algorithmic frugality (Schwartz et al., 2020; van Wynsberghe, 2021), I develop a Strategic Calibration Framework with three pillars: temporal calibration, strategic oscillation, and legacydriven adaptation. Luxury restraint is read as a demand-side analogue to algorithmic frugality. Three cases illustrate the framework. Hermès announced an Artificial Intelligence Governance Committee at its April 2025 AGM with a declared red line around creative and artisanal processes. Kering launched and quietly retired the Madeline generative-AI shopping assistant on its KNXT platform between 2023 and 2024, followed by a September 2025 CEO transition. Stella McCartney's 2019 Google Cloud sustainability pilot, whose productisation cannot be traced beyond 2020, and the firm's 2025 retirement of its Environmental Profit and Loss framework, together expose the gap between AI-for-sustainability claims and disclosed outcomes. The capacity to refuse, slow or selectively scale AI deployment is itself a higher-order capability worth theorising, and luxury offers a candid sectoral mirror for the wider RI conversation on AI.

detail.abstract: We study the value of discretionary online assortment control under limited product inventories and homogeneous multinomial logit demand. A fully dynamic assortment policy may revise the offered assortment after every customer arrival, whereas under one-shot inventory activation, the seller chooses a sellable inventory vector before the selling season, withholds all other units, and thereafter offers every product with positive remaining sellable inventory. We ask how much worst-case performance is lost when this online flexibility is replaced by a single preseason decision. We show that this restriction causes no loss in the optimal guarantee relative to the sales-based fluid benchmark. For a deterministic horizon, one-shot activation achieves the tight factor 1-1/e, matching the best possible guarantee among fully dynamic assortment policies. The policy is obtained from a revenue-ordered fluid inventory with at most one fractional component, corresponding to the boundary product, and selects between its two adjacent integer roundings based on their stochastic expected revenues. We implement this comparison using a coupled Poisson-clock estimator that directly estimates the endpoint revenue difference and an exact stockout-jump procedure, yielding a 1-1/e-ε guarantee in O(n^2 / ε^2) operations independent of the horizon length. For an IFR random horizon, a simple revenue-threshold policy achieves the analogous tight factor of 1/2. The policies also improve approximation guarantees for capacity-constrained inventory selection and joint inventory allocation across stores. Computational results show that the proposed one-shot policy performs nearly identically to strong dynamic assortment policies across a broad range of instances.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Emerging trade corridors such as the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) are increasingly framed as instruments of supply chain resilience amid recurring disruptions to established maritime chokepoints. This study examines how firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) adoption capability and digital infrastructure readiness, together with institutional policy support and perceived corridor connectivity, are hypothesised to shape supply chain visibility and, in turn, supply chain resilience and export performance among Indian exporting firms positioned to benefit from IMEC.

Design/methodology/approach: Grounded in the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and the Dynamic Capabilities View (DCV), a seven-construct reflective model was developed, together with a full PLS-SEM analytical protocol for execution in SmartPLS. Because primary fieldwork among IMEC-linked exporting firms was at an early stage at the time of writing, the analytical pipeline is demonstrated on a simulated, methodologically calibrated illustrative dataset (n = 285) constructed to reproduce realistic psychometric and structural properties. The full instrument is provided for subsequent field deployment.

Findings (simulated demonstration only): In the illustrative dataset, all seven constructs showed satisfactory convergent reliability and validity (Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability above 0.85; average variance extracted above 0.60) and discriminant validity (HTMT below 0.85). AI adoption capability, digital infrastructure readiness, and corridor connectivity perception each significantly predicted supply chain visibility, which strongly predicted supply chain resilience and, together with resilience, export performance, in the simulated data. Supply chain visibility partially mediated the simulated effects of AI and digital infrastructure on resilience. These patterns illustrate what the model would produce under the stated assumptions; they are not evidence about real Indian exporting firms.

Originality/value: This is among the first studies to integrate AI capability and digital infrastructure constructs with a corridor-specific connectivity construct within a single PLS-SEM model contextualised to IMEC, offering a validated measurement instrument and a fully worked analytical template for the empirical work that IMEC's continuing maturation will make possible.

detail.abstract: The dominant narrative around generative artificial intelligence in the workplace holds that it raises productivity. This is true but incomplete, and the incompleteness matters for how firms should invest. Drawing on Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond's (2025) landmark field study of 5,172 customer support agentspublished in the Quarterly Journal of Economicsthis paper argues that generative AI's central economic signature is not productivity growth per se but skill compression: a 34-35 percent productivity gain concentrated almost entirely among novice and low-skill workers, alongside a small but measurable quality decline among the most experienced workers who used the tool. This pattern runs contrary to the skill-biased technical change that characterized prior waves of computerization, in which new technology systematically favored already-high-skill workers. We argue this reversal has direct implications for firm-level human capital strategy, and propose a reframing of AI capital investment decisions around workforce composition rather than aggregate productivity forecasts alone.

detail.abstract: We study methods for approximating road-network distances on dense urban maps, with a focus on downstream optimization tasks such as route planning. In many applications, distances are obtained on demand from a shortest-path engine or mapping service, generating millions to billions of origin-destination queries and making distance retrieval a major computational bottleneck. We treat these systems as distance oracles and build surrogate models that approximate these distances while preserving downstream solution quality. We train neural networks using decision-agnostic and decision-focused learning by representing the map as a grid and by using network-level features. Our theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees for the grid-based approximation and derives bounds linking distance-prediction errors to downstream solution quality. We consider the asymmetric traveling salesman problem (ATSP) and the p-median problem in a real last-mile service area in Montréal with the Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) as the shortest-path oracle. Our computational study evaluates grid resolutions ranging from 50 to 250 cells along each dimension, compares multiple learning models, and tests downstream performance on optimization instances with up to 250 locations for the ATSP and 500 locations for the 𝑝-median problem. On the largest ATSP and 𝑝-median benchmarks, the strongest learned surrogates reduce the downstream gaps by about 95% relative to the Euclidean baseline. Decision-focused models trained on ATSP instances achieve the strongest ATSP performance, whereas decision-agnostic learning is stronger overall on the 𝑝-median benchmarks and is more robust across the two optimization problems.

detail.abstract: A preserved historical record can remain valid, semantically unchanged, and provenance-intact while the later process that determines which parts of that record are allowed to participate in an object-relative inquiry becomes selective, outcome-conditioned, capacity-distorted, retrieval-biased, adaptively contaminated, or otherwise improperly governed. Existing work addresses many neighboring problems: selective inclusion and outcome reporting, evidentiary admissibility and relevance, protocol specification, provenance, retrieval transparency, adaptive data analysis, and post-selection inference. Yet these mechanisms do not by themselves supply a single transition architecture for the warrant by which preserved historical material acquires candidate standing in a later inquiry. This paper formalizes that transition. It distinguishes a versioned declared inquiry universe, a valid pre-formation receipt pool, candidate-unit construction, candidate eligibility, capacity-constrained selection, downstream formative-linkage adjudication, and the integrity status of the candidate-constitution process itself. Candidate units may be single receipts, sets, ordered sequences, or configurations; construction and eligibility require independent justification; object-relative eligibility is separated from outcome-conditioned admission; unresolved eligibility is propagated through robustness over admissible resolutions; and retrieval, derived artifacts, effective information state, and adaptive system state are treated as governance-relevant when they materially alter the field presented to adjudication. The architecture also separates traceability from legitimacy and represents the final result on two independent axes: the downstream linkage result and Candidate-Constitution Integrity (CCI). The central theorem is a non-inheritance result: historical fidelity does not entail candidate-constitution integrity. Every original receipt may remain valid while the later evidentiary field is improperly constituted. Conversely, a correct downstream outcome does not retroactively validate a defective candidate-constitution process. The contribution is therefore not a new theory of selection bias. It is a formal account of candidate standing as a distinct governed transition between preserved history and later object-relative evidentiary use.

detail.abstract: The U.S. Copyright Office treats expression generated by AI as categorically unprotectable, even when a human directs the process and incorporates the output into a work. This Article argues that the Office's position rests on a mistaken model of authorship, in which the author must personally generate each element of fixed expression or at least transcribe a precise mental conception formed in advance. Neither model describes how authors actually work. Creation proceeds by trial and error. Authors generate expressive variations, often through processes they do not control, and settle on results that fulfill an intent that may itself change along the way. Photographers shooting in burst mode, Ellsworth Kelly’s randomly dropped paper fragments, and Judge Frank’s “clap of thunder” in Alfred Bell & Co. v. Catalda all show that copyright already recognizes authorship of expression the author did not deliberately generate. The Article contends that the irreducible act of authorship is adoption, meaning the choice to treat a set of sensory signals as the embodiment of one's expressive intent. The joint authorship cases support this account. They locate authorship in decision-making authority over what the work will contain, not in the generation of content. The adoption theory does not license appropriating preexisting material, because originality doctrine separately bars claims to the commons or to others' expression. On this reading, originality works like the Lockean limits on appropriation. AI output is abundant and takes nothing from the commons, so there is no principled reason to deny protection to a human author who adopts it as her own expression.

detail.abstract: For four decades, the prevailing assumption has been that information technology dissolves firm boundaries, pushing activity out of hierarchies and into markets. This article presents evidence that artificial intelligence is reversing that logic. The public reasoning of corporate leaders across AI infrastructure and frontier model development documents a consistent shift from the language of platforms and outsourcing to that of full-stack integration and infrastructure ownership: the same firms that previously justified dissolving their boundaries now justify expanding them. This article looks at the structural forces behind the shift to draw out what the pattern means for managers and corporate leaders beyond the technology frontier.

detail.abstract: AI literacy is usually taught as a transaction. A user learns to write a prompt, check the answer, protect sensitive information, and recognize a hallucination. Those skills describe one encounter at a time. Generative AI operates in a longer loop. A user's assumptions shape the prompt; the answer reshapes the next question; repeated outputs change what the user notices and accepts; AI-assisted work enters reports and the public record; later systems retrieve that material and may learn from it. Errors can come from the model, from the user, or from the two working on each other. This paper treats the person and the model as components of one coupled knowledge system and joins the literatures on model collapse, retrieval and source dependence, automation bias, cognitive offloading, sycophancy, metacognition, and AI literacy. It contributes a framework of seven paired human and machine vulnerabilities, offered as reinforcing pathways for training and research to test rather than as proven causal laws, and converts the framework into three levels of literacy and a four-stage routine that scales with the stakes of the task. The empirical anchor is a pre-registered audit of four generative search products on six Virginia public-record questions, run twice each in September 2026. Across 48 answers the products displayed 185 citations that reached 136 distinct pages; thirteen were the record itself, none documented an independent check, and 90 could not be followed from what the product showed. The audit, together with the fictional Mountains of Kong, makes the paper's central point: a well-written answer with genuine citations can still mislead when derivative sources are counted as independent evidence, or when the user and the system quietly revise the question together. The paper closes with a course scaffold built on the framework and the deposited audit data.

detail.abstract: Power-law and scale-free claims about production and supply networks carry weight beyond description. Resilience arguments, disruption-propagation models, and concentration assessments consume the fitted exponent as an input, and the methods that certified the published exponents range from current maximum-likelihood protocols with goodness-of-fit testing to log-log regression read by eye. This article audits the certification behind the claims. We assemble a verified corpus of twenty published power-law claims about production, trade, and supply networks, grade the method behind each empirical claim, and re-analyze three foundational datasets spanning four distributions under one uniform, peer-reviewed protocol, with the continuous fits cross-validated against an independent implementation and a closed-form check. The heavy-tail phenomenon largely survives: three of four re-analyzed distributions remain plausible power laws on the original claims' terms, and the canonical Zipf firm-size result reproduces almost exactly on the current census release, a structural-equivalence rather than same-data comparison. The exponents do not survive in the same way. They are method-conditioned, they do not transfer across estimators, and roughly half the corpus rests on methods uncheckable under current goodness-of-fit standards. The audit closes with a certification checklist for structure claims and a live software trap: a widely used fitting library caps continuous exponents at 3.0 by default in its current release, so true exponents above three are invisible to its default call. Structure arguments stand; exponent-magnitude arguments need re-certification.

detail.abstract: We develop an index policy for finite-horizon Bernoulli multi-armed bandits from minimax solutions to single-arm bandit (SAB) problems. Each SAB problem involves choosing between an unknown Bernoulli arm and a known reward. We show that minimizing worst-case regret of SAB problems over all non-anticipative policies admits an exact semi-infinite linear programming formulation. The resulting stopping policies offer a natural way to compare arms: the higher the known reward against which a policy continues sampling, the more promising the unknown arm. We turn this intuition into indices based on cumulative continuation probabilities, with a monotone adjustment and a reward-shortfall cap. By relating index errors to the regret of single-arm stopping policies, we establish a distribution-free regret bound of 4.45 √ KT + 10.75K for K arms and horizon T. This bound matches the minimax-optimal regret order established in the literature. The guarantee extends to rewards supported on [0, 1] through Bernoulli randomization. We also provide a finite-grid implementation with quantified approximation loss. In numerical experiments, the SAB-based index policy achieves lower worst-case regret than every tested benchmark policy across all evaluated numbers of arms and horizons, while closely matching the grid-based MAB minimax policy in the two-arm setting.

detail.abstract:
Prioritarianism is an ethical view that gives extra weight—priority—to the well-being of the worse off.  Unlike utilitarianism, which adds up well-being, prioritarianism ranks outcomes according to the sum total of concavely transformed well-being.

The existing literature about prioritarianism, in philosophy and economics, focuses on human beings.  And human-centered prioritarianism standardly uses a whole-lifetime “currency”: outcomes are ranked according to the sum total of humans’ concavely transformed lifetime well-being.

This Article considers how prioritarianism should be broadened to include all sentient animals.  It argues against animal-inclusive lifetime prioritarianism.  A whole-lifetime currency is appropriate only for an animal that is robustly intertemporally conscious: aware of itself as existing over an entire lifetime, and capable of caring, for itself, about what happens over that entire lifetime.  As far as we know, very few (if any) animals other than humans are robustly intertemporally conscious.

The Article proposes and fleshes out a novel format for animal-inclusive prioritarianism: “dual aggregation.”  Dual aggregation uses two temporal currencies: lifetime well-being for humans and other animals (if there are any) that are robustly intertemporally conscious, and momentary well-being for animals that lack robust intertemporal consciousness.

Dual aggregation is not speciesist.  It is not hierarchical; neither of the two groups of animals is assigned a higher status, or systematically upweighted, relative to the other.  Finally, dual aggregation mitigates an objection raised by the philosopher Shelly Kagan to animal-inclusive prioritarianism: namely that it leads to a (arguably counterintuitive) priority for nonhumans over badly off humans.  One upshot of dual aggregation is that animals in the lifetime-currency group who are sufficiently badly off—whose level of lifetime well-being is sufficiently low— take priority over all animals whose well-being is aggregated via the currency of momentary well-being.

detail.abstract: Imported algorithmic accountability tools fail in Westminster jurisdictions because they target the agency, not the minister. Algorithmic impact assessments, transparency standards, and AI assurance frameworks have been developed within the administrative-state frame of the United States and the regulatory-state frame of the European Union. They are now being imported, largely unmodified, into jurisdictions operating under Westminster constitutional architecture, where the minister is the constitutional accountability node and agencies advise rather than act. The import produces a structural accountability gap. The paper makes four calibrated contributions: it analyses the gap through the Westminster doctrinal frame; it identifies cross-architecture transplantation as the proximate mechanism; it treats algorithmic systems as the immediate deployment context in which the misalignment now bites; and it proposes a redesign vocabulary, accountability by constitutional fit. The imported AIA literature identifies the wrong accountability target. The gap manifests through four co-occurring patterns: abstraction, displacement, temporal, and scale, anchored to four Westminster cases drawn from the public record (Australia's Robodebt scheme, the UK Home Office visa streaming tool, the UK Ofqual A-level grading algorithm, and the decision-support systems of New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation). The redesign principle carries three operational elements: a ministerial legibility requirement, procurement-stage constitutional review, and rotation-safe decommissioning. The argument is theoretical and case selection is on the dependent variable.

detail.abstract: We study robust welfare maximization when agents may collude ex-ante—i.e., before each agent learns his values or decides whether to participate in the mechanism.  Agents and/or coalitions have property rights in that they can veto certain allocations; they can therefore threaten to punish others by holding out and refusing to participate in the mechanism.  The first-best welfare can be guaranteed if and only if the (ex-ante expected) social welfare can be divided among agents in a way that gives each coalition at least its (ex-ante expected) contribution to social welfare—such divisions comprise the anti-core of the cooperative game induced by coalitions' ex-ante expected payoffs.  Guaranteeing the first-best welfare requires making each agent's (ex-ante expected) utility robust to collusion, and anti-core payoff profiles give the utility profiles of first-best-guaranteeing mechanisms.  We also characterize the second-best welfare guarantee and the minimum subsidy needed for a first-best guarantee to be achievable.  A mechanism's welfare guarantee in our model of collusion corresponds to worst-case welfare over all perfect Bayesian equilibria of a repeated version of the mechanism in the limit in which all agents are patient.  Our implementations are robust even to collusion of which some agents may be unaware.

detail.abstract: Australian digital infrastructure debate routinely treats interstate cloud and data centre capacity as functionally national infrastructure. For ordinary commercial workloads this assumption is sound. For workloads characterised by low outage tolerance, disaster-correlated demand, sensitive data, jurisdictional accountability, or cyber-response criticality, the assumption is unverified. This paper distinguishes four concepts routinely conflated in Australian policy and procurement practice: connectivity, availability, assurance, and capability. It develops a scored workload-level assurance instrument, an unvalidated prototype offered for testing rather than a calibrated classification tool, that sorts digital workloads into three tiers (procure, federate, localise or locally assure), pairs the instrument with an order-of-magnitude cost-ofassurance band model built from analytical assumptions rather than observed costs, and applies it end-to-end to an illustrative Queensland public-sector workload. Drawing on the 2024 CrowdStrike-Falcon incident, the Optus incidents of 2022 and 2023, the 2016 Amazon Web Services Sydney availability-zone outage, and the Australian fuelsecurity response to the 2026 closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the paper tests two hypotheses: that interstate digital dependency becomes operationally riskier during systemic stress, and that Australian policy debate underprices domestic distance. Neither hypothesis is established on the public evidence available. The restoration-priority indicator cannot be directly tested, because no public Australian record shows a provider deprioritising a state during capacity scarcity, and the disaster coincidence indicator does not support the strong physical form of the claim. What support exists is indirect and conditional, and both hypotheses are presented as motivating investigation rather than as findings. Through a law-and-economics lens, the paper argues that hyperscale concentration is endogenous to demand and tax geography, that the appropriate response is workload-graded assurance rather than duplication, and that the Commonwealth Hosting Certification Framework, designed to assure ownership, control and security, leaves geographic concentration within the federation as a distinct question. Implications for public-sector procurement, investment discipline and intergovernmental coordination are developed.

detail.abstract: The National Electricity Market has two scarcity problems, and its access arrangements price both with the vocabulary of one. Peak demand sizes networks, and the firm-capacity and curtailability instruments now in play measure contribution in firm megawatts, while behind-the-meter photovoltaics have created a second and opposite scarcity at midday, when operational demand falls so low that system security binds. This paper asks what access instrument would carry the value of relieving that trough to the siting and operating decisions of large flexible loads, and whether it would outperform the firm-capacity covenant and the Commonwealth's net-generator obligation. It offers preliminary evidence and a candidate instrument, and it argues neither as settled. A preliminary decomposition of midday surplus, independently reproduced and reported as specification-sensitive, finds security-coincident hours concentrated in the regions that already hold the compute. It is the local counterpart of a Californian curtailment decomposition, and the searches conducted for this paper found no published Australian precedent. A reproduction of a consumer-energyadvocacy consultancy's minimum-demand figure finds it understates the measure the consultancy itself chose. The paper sketches a two-limb System-Contribution Connection, curtailable at peak and present at the trough, names the conditions under which it would work, and sets out the research agenda a full test would require.

detail.abstract: Does industry-level economic information predict future equity returns? Using 1,049 monthly measures of production, employment, hours worked, sales, and inventories across 426 U.S. industries, we construct an Industry Input-Output Propagation Network. The network predicts aggregate market monthly returns with an out-of-sample R 2 of 23.8%, with predictability concentrated in upstream industries such as manufacturing, transportation, and mining. Production and sales transmit positive demand signals, while employment transmits more negative signals than hours worked despite the two measuring closely related labor inputs. These findings suggest that production networks are an important mechanism through which real economic information is gradually incorporated into equity prices.

detail.abstract: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) link the primary and secondary markets through blockchain's traceability, enabling creators to earn resale royalties and benefit from a community of consumers who hold their NFTs long-term. As a key tokenomics mechanism, airdrops are widely used to influence consumers' postpurchase decisions between holding and reselling. Yet the existing literature does not examine how creators should choose among the various airdrop tools available to balance long-term holding, royalty generation, and consumer base growth. We develop a two-period model in which a creator earns revenue not only from the primary market but also from the secondary market through resale royalties. The model captures consumers' holding-versus-reselling decisions and the community effect arising from the holder base. We examine the case in which the creator has the option of using the following airdrop tools: a bounty airdrop that rewards promotional effort and expands the pool of potential consumers; or a holder airdrop that rewards NFT ownership at a specific snapshot date. We find that a bounty airdrop is the optimal airdrop tool when long-term NFT ownership is not very attractive. Otherwise, a holder airdrop is the better airdrop tool, particularly when the community effect is strong. We further show that, counterintuitively, consumers can be worse off as the community effect strengthens, as the bounty reward increases, or as promotional activities become more effective. We also find that consumers are always better off with holder airdrops but can be worse off with bounty airdrops. The managerial implications of our paper are twofold. First, creators should choose the airdrop tool based on the NFT's retention value and the stage of community development. Second, regulators should balance the objective of expanding participation in digital economies with the need to protect consumer surplus. Specifically, while bounty airdrops can attract new participants and stimulate market activity, they would also raise secondary-market prices, indicating that stronger promotional incentives may reduce consumer surplus.

detail.abstract: Bitcoin-altcoin correlation is strong, but Bitcoin's short-horizon predictive lead is close to zero. Using two years (2024-2026) of hourly and 4-hour Binance data for Bitcoin and nine major altcoins, we separate these two claims-usually conflated-and locate where leadership actually lives. Contemporaneous return correlation averages 0.772, while the one-hour-ahead correlation is approximately 0.006, and Holm-corrected Granger tests leave no robust one-way hourly lead. Leadership exists instead at the trend-regime level: after a Bitcoin regime flip, altcoins that currently disagree with Bitcoin's regime converge to it within 24 hours at a rate 15.1 percentage points above a matched, disagreementconditioned control (out-of-sample, p<0.001). The effect is positive in five of five walkforward folds, in fifteen of fifteen parameter specifications, in every yearly subsample, under non-overlapping events, and replicates on a second exchange in a second quote currency-yet trading it returns-0.343% per event after realistic costs. A fourarchitecture ensemble (LSTM, XGBoost, Transformer, KAN) trained on the same regime target reproduces the conclusion independently: 81% regime classification F1 decomposes into 52% directional accuracy and cost-negative signals. We further document a measured Goodhart effect in continuously trained systems: any metric used to accept model updates becomes unusable for ensemble calibration. Predictability and profitability are distinct properties, and classification metrics without economic decomposition systematically overstate cryptocurrency forecastability.

detail.abstract: This working paper develops a quantitative accounting framework for assessing the internal consistency of the capital-formation cycle in the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language model (LLM) industry as of 2026. Three components are formalised. First, a bottom-up engineering cost model for the inference of frontier ultra-large models (parameter counts of the order of 2.8 × 10 12) is used to bound the implied gap between the marginal compute cost and observed end-user prices; under unbatched single-stream execution the implied cost-to-revenue ratio reaches approximately 3,950×, which falls to a range of roughly 30×-100× once dynamic batching and low-precision quantisation are accounted for. Second, a two-equation exponential divergence model of infrastructure capital expenditure and end-market AI revenue is calibrated on 2023-2026 public disclosures and third-party estimates, yielding an implied annual funding gap in excess of USD 600 billion. Third, an efficiency-adjusted demand identity is derived, showing that when the growth rate of tokens-per-accelerator efficiency exceeds the growth rate of token demand, net physical accelerator demand contracts-a mechanism we label the inverted Jevons regime. These components are combined with a Cash Flow-to-CapEx Sustainability Ratio (CFSR) and with publicly disclosed intra-ecosystem investment and procurement commitments to characterise the conditions under which the observed expenditure trajectory ceases to be organically fundable. A stylized, deliberately non-firm-specific liquidity-depletion model illustrates the timing of the transition to external financing dependence. The paper concludes with a set of falsifiable predictions, a discussion of alternative hypotheses under which no repricing occurs, and implications for financial-stability monitoring and corporate disclosure. The paper is an analytical exercise in industrial and financial economics; it contains no investment recommendation.

detail.abstract: Financial markets are often assumed to incorporate Federal Reserve policy decisions instantaneously. Yet it remains unclear whether markets fully absorb policy-relevant information at the moment of release, or whether information continues to be revealed as the policy narrative unfolds across sequential communications. I construct a novel measure of policy communication shocks, the Communication Divergence Signal (CDS), which captures semantic, tonal, and framing shifts across sequential FOMC communications. Using large language models and high-frequency event-study methods, I show that communication divergence generates significant and persistent movements in intraday asset prices and abnormal trading volume. Abnormal trading volume is measured relative to non-announcement benchmarks at the same intraday horizon, isolating excess trading activity associated with information arrival. I further document systematic responses in daily open interest, consistent with belief updating and position reallocation rather than transitory liquidity provision. These findings highlight the role of communication sequencing and framing in shaping price discovery and trading dynamics across financial markets.

detail.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence, automation, energy and production technologies renew claims that productive scarcity may become less binding. Yet productive abundance does not necessarily translate into secure human abundance, and high present consumption does not ensure sustainability. This conceptual theory-synthesis paper develops Sustainable Abundance (SA) Theory as an integrative explanatory framework for assessing when productive capacity becomes a durable state of Need Security, Substantive Capability Access, and Ecological Compatibility. Full SA requires these three constitutive domains jointly; durability over a stated horizon and system-boundary integrity qualify the classification. Productive potential is an antecedent rather than part of the state, and flourishing remains a possible downstream outcome. Six propositions specify testable relationships involving institutional conversion, provisioning power and safeguards, rebound and externalisation, time-dividend conversion, activity-allocation diversity, and durability under shock or gradual stress. A bounded adversarial prior-art comparison identifies substantial component-level precedents and several close rival architectures; the proposed contribution is therefore the integration, ordering, qualification and empirical contestability of the complete architecture rather than invention of its ingredients. A stylised diagnostic application shows how high-output systems can fail different N, C, E or boundary tests. Measurement should begin with a threshold-based, non-compensatory dashboard, explicit ecological allocation rules and subgroup coverage checks; a composite SA Index is reserved for later construct validation.

detail.abstract: The trades disclosed under the STOCK Act by the household of Representative Nancy Pelosi are widely presented as evidence that a legislator can anticipate acts of Congress and beat the market. This paper tests the claim with three event-study designs on the complete record of 65 Periodic Transaction Reports filed between 2014 and 2026 (227 transactions, 117 discretionary events after cleaning, 68 involving long call options). First, timing: signed abnormal returns after the trades are nil at 5, 20 and 60 sessions; over one year purchases beat the S&P 500 by 15.9 per cent but the Nasdaq-100 by 12.2, and the stocks sold went on to outperform by 24.5 per cent, so that purchases and sales together earn nothing against either benchmark. Second, disclosure: no abnormal volume or return when the filings become public, including in 2021–2026 when aggregators publish them within hours. Third, proximity: of 88 act–ticker pairs built from 42 federal acts affecting the traded stocks (votes, enactments, AI-chip export controls, antitrust actions), 3 were preceded within 60 days by a trade in the expected direction, against 4.4 expected under random dates, and 8 by a trade in the opposite direction. The household buys after declines and holds a leveraged, concentrated position in large-cap technology through a bull market; the record contains no trace of informed timing. detail.abstract: Cost accounting for AI infrastructure typically treats a hardware unit as a single capital input, acquired once and consumed by the workload it was purchased for. This paper argues that treatment omits two related facts. First, a GPU or server can remain physically functional for years after it stops being the economically competitive choice for the specific AI workload it was acquired for, because successive hardware generations improve performance per watt and cost per token faster than physical components fail. Second, hardware displaced from that original workload does not typically stop generating economic or material value; it is commonly resold, redeployed to less demanding computing roles, or eventually recovered for components and materials. Treating a single "useful life" figure as sufficient, and treating an asset's first application as its only economically relevant use, understates and overstates AI's resource burden respectively, and the two errors partially offset in ways current accounting frameworks do not make visible. This paper makes three contributions. First, it develops a temporal model of AI hardware useful life that distinguishes physical durability from workload-specific economic competitiveness, and introduces Effective Hardware Life Cost (EHLC) as a conceptual counterpart to Hardware Capital Cost. Second, it proposes a two-ledger accounting structure that keeps a primary-product ledger, tracking the resource-to-return chain for an AI system's original deployment, separate from a byproduct ledger tracking value the same physical assets generate after leaving that deployment. Third, it applies this structure to the resource-allocation question raised by increasingly computeintensive multi-agent architectures, reframing the relevant comparison from token cost per task to the marginal value of directing constrained hardware toward additional primary-product compute versus toward the secondary uses the byproduct ledger tracks. The paper is grounded in public evidence: divergent 2025 depreciation-schedule revisions at Amazon and Meta, vendor-disclosed generational performance and embodied-carbon data, and reported secondary-market pricing for retired accelerators. It does not estimate an empirical allocation of embodied resource cost between primary and secondary use; it identifies the allocation problem, proposes candidate allocation bases, and leaves their empirical resolution to subsequent research. The paper's scope is conceptual and structural rather than econometric, and its limitations are stated explicitly in Section 8.

detail.abstract: Corporate restructuring scholarship has traditionally examined financial distress through identifiable legal events, institutional procedures and the strategic behaviour of individual actors. While these perspectives have generated a sophisticated body of literature, they largely assume that the restructuring process begins when financial distress becomes legally recognisable. This Article argues that an analytically significant stage precedes that moment and has remained conceptually underexplored. The Article develops the Insolvency Undertow Theory, an explanatory framework describing the gradual transformation of a distressed firm's commercial environment before formal restructuring proceedings commence. Rather than emerging from coordinated action or legal intervention, this transformation results from the cumulative effect of ordinary commercial decisions independently taken by lenders, suppliers, customers, insurers and other market participants. Individually, these decisions are commercially rational and legally unremarkable. Collectively, however, they progressively alter the conditions under which corporate rescue may later be attempted. The theory distinguishes between legal continuity and commercial continuity, arguing that contractual rights and legal relationships may remain formally unchanged while the commercial foundations supporting restructuring steadily deteriorate. It further explains why businesses with comparable financial characteristics frequently enter restructuring proceedings under markedly different practical conditions despite being subject to the same legal framework. From this perspective, formal insolvency proceedings do not mark the beginning of restructuring but instead represent the point at which a market transformation that has already unfolded becomes visible to the legal system. The Article positions the Insolvency Undertow Theory as an explanatory contribution to insolvency scholarship rather than a proposal for legislative reform. By identifying a previously untheorised phase in the chronology of corporate restructuring, it provides a conceptual framework capable of integrating fragmented observations found across insolvency law, financial distress literature and commercial practice into a coherent account of pre-insolvency market transformation.

detail.abstract: A dwelling is the smallest object that holds territory, boundary, access, exclusion, ownership, privacy, shelter, safety, services, activity, memory, identity, value, inheritance and permanence at the same moment. This article asks how such an object forms from many simple physical and computational elements, and what remains of ownership once its geometry is free to change. The answer is built rather than described. One structured file declares a house as modules, edge slots, capabilities, sensors, actuators, activity contracts, a ledger of holders and a set of safety invariants; four layers read that same file. A relational layer answers every question about the house as a query over its graph-zones, travel distance to a way out, load paths to ground, and what a zone offers in area, span, illuminance, air change rate, thermal band, acoustic separation, water and surface. A swarm layer gives every cell and every slot an agent that holds its own state, talks where it touches and reads nothing wider: a zone label, a distance to a way out, a set of capability holders and a proposal with its votes all converge by local agreement, and a quorum commits. A safety kernel sits below both, with seven invariants answered at proposal and again at commit. Property is written as four invariants over a ledger-identity, capability envelope as a product of ratios, access, and severability-so that a reconfiguration which changes the plan entirely leaves tenure intact, while one that takes away a holder's means of acting is refused. Twenty-two logged rows report what the house does when its busiest agent leaves, when a third of its actuators stop, when its network splits, when every identifier is scrambled, when the power goes, when the occupant starts using a wheelchair, when five columns are lost and when the exits are locked. The same rules run on three plans of different shape, cell size, module count and topology, measured against a planner that sees everything. Activity conditions carry published figures: 300 lux of daylight provision, four air changes an hour of purge ventilation, an operative band of 20 to 24 degrees, 45 decibels between dwellings, 850 millimetres of clear door width and a 1500 millimetre turning circle, the last of which sets the cell at 1.5 metres. A parameterised cost model then asks whether a house like this is cheaper and faster, and answers in the unit a household lives in: twenty-six contract-hours a day cost 0.79, 0.54 and 0.27 dollars a contract-hour across a room-per-contract plan, a conventional plan and a reconfigurable one, while the reconfigurable plan is the dearest of the three per square metre. The answer turns on one assumption-a household accepting about 108 per cent of the conventional plan's area or less-rather than on the price of a module, which would have to reach forty-eight times the figure used here before the ranking changed. On speed the claim is about a change: one panel moves in 0.4 minutes against eleven hours of trade work. The article closes with a room that can be built from named parts, and with the thirteen ways the whole proposal could be shown wrong.

detail.abstract: Existing critiques of backtested alpha in agentic trading systems correctly diagnose the problem-lookahead bias, interface-driven behavior, absence of stable directional edge-but stop short of prescribing what a practitioner should do before committing capital. Reporting standards such as the P1-P6 protocol evaluate a claim after the fact; they do not tell an engineer when or how to move a system from backtest to live capital. This paper proposes a staged-capital evaluation protocol: zero-weight shadow validation, forward paper-testing on live data, minimal live capital gated by deterministic and mechanical exit logic, and gradual scaling gated by pre-registered statistical tests. We ground the protocol's central design choice-that exit and sizing logic must be mechanical rather than modelmediated-in production evidence showing that forcing an agent to self-report risk exposure before entry changed none of its behavior, and that a fixed mechanical stop/target bracket outperformed discretionary exits. We corroborate the shadow-validation stage with an independent engineering observation from a real institutional deployment. We conclude that the missing piece in agentic trading evaluation is not more reporting theory but a deployable, falsifiable rollout protocol.

detail.abstract:
Construction megaprojects are chronically impaired by multi-tier supply chain vulnerabilities, systemic logistical friction, and cascading schedule overruns that trigger multi-million-dollar disputes and severe commercial claims. Conventional construction supply chain risk management (CSCRM) relies almost exclusively on static, qualitative risk registers compiled during pre-tender planning, infrequent monthly audits, and retrospective Critical Path Method (CPM) progress updates in Oracle Primavera P6. These legacy mechanisms are fundamentally reactive; they detect procurement disruptions only after site delivery milestones have failed, leaving project controls teams with depleted float, exorbitant acceleration costs, and prolonged delay exposures. To resolve this structural operational bottleneck, this study develops, mathematically formulates, and empirically validates an end-to-end framework titled the Predictive Supply Chain Risk Governance (PSCRG) model. The PSCRG framework establishes a continuous cyber-physical feedback loop integrating multimodal enterprise telemetry-spanning 4D/5D Building Information Modeling (BIM), Internet of Things (IoT) logistical sensors, automated Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel tracking, enterprise resource planning (ERP) financials, and Primavera P6 CPM logic-with high-dimensional machine learning and Dynamic Bayesian Belief Networks (BBN).
The predictive core incorporates Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) recurrent neural networks to generate calibrated, asymmetric quantile distributions of material lead-time variance (Q_tau) and evaluate sub-tier vendor insolvency probabilities (P(Def)). Predicted supply shocks are mapped directly onto the project schedule network DAG to quantify dynamic critical path float dissipation, schedule elasticity (eta_SC), and downstream delay propagation. The framework incorporates an automated contractual governance engine grounded in FIDIC (1999/2017) and NEC4 standard forms, triggering verifiable Advance Warning Notices and optimizing proactive mitigation interventions via a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) cost-loss optimization protocol.
The PSCRG architecture was empirically deployed and validated across a longitudinal 48-month dataset from a completed $1.2 billion multi-facility infrastructure and high-rise complex megaproject encompassing 12,450 CPM activities, 42 primary contractors, and 18 highly critical, long-lead procurement packages. The stacking ensemble predictive model demonstrated superior forecasting accuracy over traditional CPM and linear baselines, achieving a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 5.8 calendar days (Mean Absolute Percentage Error [MAPE] of 3.84%) on lead times exceeding 180 days, and an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.952 in identifying vendor delivery distress. The framework detected upstream delivery failures an average of 54.2 calendar days prior to conventional monthly schedule updates, preserved 34.8% of available critical path float, and avoided an estimated $18.4 million in liquidated ascertained damages (LADs) and contractor prolongation overheads. This study bridges the long-standing divide between computational data science, critical path schedule analytics, and enforceable megaproject contractual governance.

detail.abstract: Supply chain disruptions create substantial information-processing challenges: organizations must detect emerging signals, interpret incomplete information, and make timely decisions under uncertainty. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has increasingly been proposed to support supply chain sensing and decision making, while Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds generative outputs in retrieved, contextually relevant information. Yet the organizational role of retrieval-grounding remains less developed than the broader literature on AI-enabled supply chain visibility, sensemaking, and resilience. This study develops a conceptual framework explaining how RAG capability may contribute to supply chain resilience through organizational sensemaking. Drawing on Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), the framework distinguishes AI-enabled sensing from AI-enabled sensemaking and positions RAG capability as a specific capability configuration within the broader GenAI capability. It proposes that GenAI and RAG capabilities support AI-enabled sensing, that sensing contributes to sensemaking, that sensemaking improves decision quality, that decision quality supports organizational agility, and that organizational agility contributes to supply chain resilience. The framework further proposes a direct relationship between RAG capability and AI-enabled sensemaking-its focal contribution. The central theoretical contribution is to conceptualize retrieval-grounding as an organizational information-grounding mechanism: a way for generative AI to connect disruption-related information with current, relevant, and context-specific evidence that can support organizational understanding. The framework offers a basis for future empirical research testing whether RAG capability produces sensemaking effects that are distinguishable from broader GenAI capability and AI-enabled sensing.

detail.abstract: Planning public fast charging networks necessitates the simultaneous representation of road congestion, station  queues, and users’ endogenous route station choices. When these mechanisms are modeled conjointly, however, the planning consequences attributable specifically to users’ responsiveness to charging station waiting can become  difficult to disentangle from the broader effects of congestion and infrastructure provision. This study develops a unified bilevel framework to elucidate the conditional planning consequences of incorporating flow dependent expected station waiting into generalized route station cost. At the upper level, the planner determines candidate site activation and discrete port capacity, whereas the lower level characterizes congestion dependent route station equilibrium in conjunction with multiserver station queues. Two behavioral specifications are differentiated exclusively through the indicator η. Expected station waiting is omitted from generalized user cost when η = 0 and incorporated when η = 1, while physical station waiting, queue stability requirements, planner objectives, design constraints, and numerical procedures remain invariant. For each scenario, the ensuing infrastructure designs are  scrutinized through changes in candidate site selection, installed port capacity, equilibrium route station flows, road link flows, station arrival rates, station choice distributions, expected waiting, utilization, investment, and operational performance. Both designs are subsequently reassigned under an identical waiting responsive evaluator, thereby precluding performance differences from being confounded by disparate behavioral assumptions. The common evaluation further decomposes operational differences into road travel, charging service, and station waiting  components, furnishing a more explicit account of the mechanisms underlying the observed performance divergence. The formulation consequently delineates lower level equilibrium redistribution from upper level location and capacity adjustments and provides a systematic basis for ascertaining whether waiting responsive assignment becomes sufficiently consequential to alter charging network planning outcomes. It further establishes a commensurate basis for identifying the circumstances under which a waiting unresponsive specification yields planning outcomes comparable to those obtained when users explicitly respond to station waiting.

detail.abstract:
The implementation of the OECD's Pillar Two global minimum tax has prompted renewed debate regarding the future of tax competition and the effectiveness of location-based tax incentives. Conventional analysis suggests that multinational enterprises (MNEs) subject to a minimum effective tax rate of 15 percent should place less weight on low corporate tax rates when making location decisions. However, the continued uptake of Saudi Arabia's Regional Headquarters (RHQ) programme presents a potentially interesting case. Official figures indicate that RHQ registrations have grown rapidly and have exceeded the programme's initial policy targets ahead of schedule. [attorney.sa], [arnifi.com]

This paper examines whether Pillar Two materially alters the economic rationale for establishing an RHQ in Saudi Arabia. It develops a Net Locational Value (NLV) framework that evaluates relocation decisions as the combined effect of four factors: corporate income tax benefits, withholding tax benefits, market-access benefits, and the costs associated with establishing and maintaining regional headquarters operations. The framework is then applied to the Saudi RHQ regime as an illustrative case study.

The analysis suggests that the impact of Pillar Two differs across the components of the RHQ package. For many in-scope multinational groups, the value of the corporate income tax incentive may be reduced by Pillar Two's minimum-tax mechanisms. By contrast, withholding tax benefits are not directly affected by Pillar Two, although their economic value depends on the tax position of the recipient and the availability of foreign tax credits in the parent jurisdiction. In addition, certain non-tax advantages, including access to segments of government procurement and broader commercial opportunities in the Saudi market, operate independently of Pillar Two and may continue to influence location decisions. Government procurement restrictions applicable to multinational groups without a Saudi RHQ have been in force since January 2024, subject to a number of regulatory exemptions. [cms.law], [khanconsultant.com]

The paper argues that the effects of Pillar Two should be assessed at the level of individual incentive mechanisms rather than at the level of a headline tax rate. The central finding is that reduced sensitivity to corporate income tax rates does not necessarily imply reduced incentives to relocate. More broadly, the study suggests that the introduction of a global minimum tax may alter the composition of jurisdictional competition without eliminating it, as governments increasingly rely on non-rate advantages and location-specific benefits to attract regional business activity.

A minimum-day condition, daily-loss limit, consistency test, trailing drawdown, payout buffer, or payout cap can change the outcome even when the trader, price path, nominal target, and nominal drawdown are identical. This paper measures those effects using a common-path rule engine. It extends the participant-value analysis in Matilla Serrano (2026b) and the selection analysis in Matilla Serrano (2026c). The same simulated profit-and-loss paths are applied to two benchmarks, six one-rule counterfactuals, and three synthetic contract bundles. The bundles are market-informed archetypes, not copies of named providers.
The simulation uses six latent trader types, 30,000 antithetic paths per type and stage, a 20-day horizon, and a population containing 20% positive-drift types. All contracts share a $3,000 target and $2,000 nominal drawdown, so their Target-to-Drawdown Ratio is 1.5. Nevertheless, outcomes differ sharply. The ideal realistic benchmark passes 28.59% of population paths and produces a first payout on 9.72% of purchased attempts. A static package with minimum days, a 50% consistency limit, and payout constraints reduces those rates to 23.45% and 6.57%. An end-of-day trailing package reduces them to 17.16% and 3.76%. A stricter intraday-trailing package reduces them to 5.04% and 0.56%. Participant expected cash flow moves from +$143.96 in the ideal realistic benchmark to +$4.85, −$39.48, and −$87.48 in the three bundles.
Rules also change who survives. Conditional on being selected, positive-drift traders constitute 32.07% of passers and 42.96% of payout events in the ideal benchmark. Those conditional shares rise to 45.75% and 74.35% in the strictest bundle. This does not mean that the strictest bundle improves outcomes for the population as a whole. Its pass and payout-event rates are far lower, and it rejects many positive-drift paths. Among one-rule counterfactuals, the $1,000 daily-loss limit has the largest effect on pass probability and is sufficient to reverse participant expected value. The results show why contract comparisons based only on target, drawdown, or nominal account size can fail. Rule packages are nonlinear, path-dependent systems. Their effects should be measured on common paths, both one rule at a time and as complete bundles.

detail.abstract:
Abstract

Nigeria has emerged as one of Africa's most dynamic financial technology (FinTech) ecosystems, driven by high mobile penetration, youthful demographics, and rising demand for accessible digital financial services, with the country attracting the largest share of the continent's FinTech investment deals. This growth, however, has been accompanied by significant regulatory and consumer-protection challenges, particularly within the digital lending subsector, where unethical practices such as data privacy breaches, harassment-based debt recovery, and unlicensed operations have proliferated. This work examines the evolving legal and institutional architecture governing FinTech and digital lending in Nigeria, focusing on the roles of the Federal Consumer and Competition Protection Commission (FCCPC), the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), and the Nigerian Data Protection Commission (NDPC), including recent instruments such as the Digital, Electronic, Online or Non-Traditional Consumer Lending Regulations 2025. Drawing on judicial precedents, enforcement actions, and high-profile cases including the delisting of dozens of loan applications and the regulatory dispute involving Binance, the paper argues that regulatory compliance is no longer merely a legal obligation but a determinant of competitive survival within Nigeria's FinTech industry. It contends that firms treating compliance as a peripheral cost rather than a core governance function face disproportionate operational, reputational, and financial risk. The paper concludes by advocating for stronger enforcement of existing frameworks, deeper integration of compliance into corporate strategy, and the eventual development of a comprehensive, dedicated FinTech statute aligned with global best practices to sustain Nigeria's digital financial inclusion gains.

detail.abstract: The global memory semiconductor industry, historically characterized by volatile boom-bust cycles driven by supply-demand mismatches, is undergoing a fundamental structural transformation. This paper argues that three converging forces are reshaping memory manufacturing in ways that may permanently alter its cyclical nature: the artificial intelligence revolution's insatiable demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the proliferation of hyperscale data centers, and accelerating geopolitical fragmentation of semiconductor supply chains. Written by someone who follows the semiconductor industry closely out of personal interest rather than as a formal research program, this analysis examines how HBM demand, projected to grow from approximately $35 billion in 2025 to over $100 billion by 2028, is creating structural supply constraints unlike previous cycles. A single NVIDIA H100 GPU requires 80GB of HBM, while next-generation AI accelerators may demand 288GB or more, fundamentally shifting the memorycompute ratio in modern systems. Unlike commodity DRAM's historical oversupply patterns, HBM's technical complexity (with yields estimated at 60-70% versus 90%+ for standard DRAM), limited supplier base (three manufacturers supplying >95% market demand), and advanced packaging bottlenecks create persistent supply tightness. Simultaneously, the US CHIPS Act ($52.7 billion in semiconductor incentives), alongside parallel initiatives in the EU, Japan, and Korea, is catalyzing geographic redistribution of memory manufacturing across every major producer, not just one. Micron’s planned Idaho and New York fab expansions represent over $100 billion in committed investment, observed firsthand by the author; but the same redistribution is visible at SK hynix, which is committing up to $16 billion in new capacity at its Yongin cluster in Korea alone and building its first US site in Indiana, at Samsung, which is investing $17 billion in a Taylor, Texas fab now targeted for 2027, at TSMC, whose Arizona commitment has grown to $265 billion, and at Kioxia and Western Digital in Japan, whose joint capital expenditure is set to rise 66% through 2028. This paper examines that redistribution holistically across all major producers rather than through any single company’s lens. This paper presents a leadership mapping across HBM, DRAM, NAND, and advanced packaging, followed by a three-horizon outlook examining near-term dynamics (2026–2030), mid-term architectural transitions (2030–2035), and long-term scenarios (2035–2040+) including memory-centric computing paradigms and sovereign semiconductor ecosystems.

detail.abstract: Strategic foresight increasingly uses probability language to communicate scenario likelihoods, yet most frameworks lack the governance architecture needed to make such claims auditable, updateable, and defensible under scrutiny. Existing approaches, including weighted scoring models, narrative Delphi, and probabilistic cross-impact analysis, each satisfy at most two of three requirements simultaneously: separating driver significance from evidential confidence, linking probability bands to structured evidence, and maintaining a provenance record auditable to individual items and reviewers. This paper introduces LOGOS (Layered Output for Governed Operational Scenarios), a two-layer architecture that addresses this gap. The first layer scores each high-level factor (HLF) for strategic significance and evidential confidence, producing a priority weight that drives the scenario probabilities and a wildcard weight published as a separate register, so that thinly evidenced but strategically consequential drivers remain visible whatever their probability share. The second layer converts validated evidence into signed evidence signals, combines these with expertelicited alignment coefficients, and transforms resulting scenario affinity scores into probability bands subject to an outside-model reserve and explicit governance controls. A parsimonious structured expert judgement protocol, based on Cooke's Classical Model and the IDEA elicitation process, ensures expert weights are performancebased rather than status-based. A synthetic worked example demonstrates the full computation path, showing priority rankings are robust to ±0.10 weight perturbations (minimum Spearman rank correlation = 0.94) and that governance controls respond correctly to surprise-event signals. LOGOS provides a practically deployable bridge between foresight craft and operational probability language that is compatible with public-sector AI governance requirements.

detail.abstract: This study employs a convergent mixed-methods exploratory design to examine the socio-technical determinants influencing healthcare professionals’ acceptance of Ambient Intelligence (AmI) for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH). An extended Technology Acceptance Model was evaluated across three context-specific clinical hazard scenarios and a pooled model using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), complemented by hybrid thematic analysis of qualitative responses. Quantitative findings identified perceived usefulness (PU) as the most consistent predictor of behavioural intention (BI), with significant positive associations across all scenarios and the pooled model. Perceived ease of use (PEOU) was not directly associated with BI but was positively associated with PU across all scenarios; significant indirect PEOU → PU → BI effects were observed in Scenarios B and C. Trust (TR) was significantly associated with BI only in Scenario B, while privacy concerns (PCON) were not significant direct predictors. The pooled model indicated a negative but non-significant shift work × PU interaction. Qualitative findings contextualized these patterns, highlighting system utility, error reduction and output optimization as key acceptance considerations, while identifying an intrusiveness threshold beyond which monitoring may disrupt established workflows. Participants also expressed surveillance and data-governance concerns, alongside expectations for transparency and user control. Additional themes addressed ergonomic and well-being support, infrastructure and training limitations, and the demands of high-stress clinical environments. Overall, the findings indicate that responsible AmI-OSH implementation should prioritize demonstrated safety utility, workflow-sensitive design, transparent data governance, and meaningful user control.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence disrupts a longstanding relationship between the quality of an artifact and the competence of the person presenting it. Once AI-generated work exceeds the independent productive or evaluative capacity of the people responsible for it, organizations risk substituting procedural compliance for substantive verification. This research note develops a framework for diagnosing that problem. It first distinguishes constitutive, load-bearing, safely delegable, and technologically contingent capacities. It then distinguishes three modes of AI use: amplification, scaffolding, and substitution. The framework is applied to the pipeline problem: the possibility that automating junior production work may preserve present performance while eroding the formation of future expert reviewers. detail.abstract: This study examines why cash remains common among respondents in the Lebanon Global Findex data even though internet use is widespread. detail.abstract: Between February and September 2026, a war between the United States/Israel and Iran produced the most severe disruption to global oil-transit infrastructure since the 1980s Tanker War. The conflict opened with the assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader on 28 February and a near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz; it then moved through an eight-month cycle of ceasefires, a signed memorandum of understanding, and renewed fighting, before a Houthi campaign against the Bab al-Mandab Strait and a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West (Petroline) pipeline converged in early-to-mid September. Brent crude oscillated accordingly-spiking to a closing high of $118.03 in late April, falling to $73.74 by 24 June as a diplomatic memorandum briefly reopened Hormuz, and climbing back above $104 by 11 September-but the price and policy response to each episode was not proportional to its severity in barrel or casualty terms. This paper develops a redundancy-erosion argument: prices and great-power responses react most sharply not to attacks on primary chokepoints per se, but to attacks that credibly threaten the substitute routes and buffers that markets and states have been relying on to absorb a primary disruption. We test this against a compiled, citation-verifiable dataset of 40 dated Brent price observations and a simple eventwindow regression with heteroskedasticity-and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors, alongside process tracing of United States, Chinese, and Gulf-state responses and a comparison case (the 2019 Abqaiq-Khurais attacks) external to the current conflict. The evidence assembled here is consistent with the redundancy-erosion account-the pipeline strike produced the fastest rate of price appreciation of any episode examined despite threatening a smaller nominal volume than the Hormuz closure-but we are explicit throughout about the limits of a sparse, pressderived price series, about a leadership assassination and a signed-and-collapsed ceasefire that complicate any account of Iran as a unitary strategic actor, and about a rival, not-yet-excluded explanation in which price movements track perceived ceasefire probability rather than physical redundancy status. We close with implications for energy-security theory, coercive bargaining, and the design of strategic reserves and alternative routing.

detail.abstract: Perishable-industry firms-seafood processing, fresh produce, and other short-shelf-life operations routinely face a structural tension between operational speed and financial control. The conventional response, a sequential hierarchy in which Operations reports through Accounts or Finance (Top → Accounts → Operations), subordinates time-critical operational decisions to a control function optimized for stability and periodic review, producing decision latency that perishable assets cannot absorb. An alternative frequently proposed in practice-dual reporting lines or parallel authority between Finance and Operations-is shown, drawing on the matrix-organization literature, to fail under precisely the time pressure that perishable operations generate, producing role conflict and hollow authority rather than genuine dual control. This paper introduces the Perishability Concurrent Governance (PCG) model, which resolves the tension through sequenced single authority: Operations holds sole, real-time decision rights within boundaries set in advance by Accounts, drawing on Simons' Levers of Control framework, with Accounts reviewing and recalibrating those boundaries after the fact rather than co-deciding during. The model integrates contingency theory, supply-chain-fit theory, classical authority-responsibility theory, and matrix-organization failure research into five testable propositions. Implications for governance design in perishable operations, and an agenda for empirical validation, are discussed.

detail.abstract: A floor plan freezes possibility. It assigns sleeping here and cooking there, and it assigns them once, for the life of the building. This paper asks what private property becomes when that assignment can be undone safely and repeatedly. A dwelling is described as two coupled graphs: a physical graph of elements and the relations currently made between them, and a property graph of actors and the incidents they hold over objects. Regions, activities and agents are computed from the first at the moment of asking, and the description leaves every room unnamed. Fourteen experiments and fifty-two counterfactuals are run across two dwellings, eleven rights regimes and eight household demands. Three results carry the argument. Releasing the plan raises the activities a dwelling carries at one time from five to six for a household of four and from two to five for a household that hosts, while a dwelling of 119 square metres holding its plan carries three. Replacing 83 per cent of a dwelling's matter across eight rounds of maintenance and reconfiguration leaves all eight kernel invariants intact and the identifier, the plot relation and the rights schedule unchanged. And of fifty-two counterfactuals, the seven that moved the property itself all touched an incident or a relation, and none touched a shape. A ten-field property kernel is proposed, a Dynamic Property Capacity reading is offered as a candidate and read beside a partial order, and an observatory page carries every state. The paper states what would falsify each claim, and reports the places where the reading came back negative.
